title: Patrick Devine - 2D Sprites with Unicode and Golang
speaker: Patrick Devine
summary: Patrick Devine shows 'stupid terminal tricks' for drawing animated 2D sprites in a terminal using a Go ASCII sprite library he wrote. He explains the clear-update-draw animation loop, adds a timer to match NES Tetris frame timing in a terminal Tetris homage, and uses Unicode quadrant block characters to get four pixels per character cell. He demos a Space Invaders clone and a terminal recreation of Super Mario Bros level 1-1, and discusses color limits, font and line-spacing requirements, and terminal differences across Linux, macOS and Windows.

insights.claim: Devine's Go terminal sprite library animates sprites with a simple loop of clearing the screen, updating sprite positions and redrawing, repeated forever.
insights.detail: His first demo bounced several Docker whale sprites around the terminal; the main source of lag was the terminal's size. In Q&A he says he relies on tmux to avoid actually doing full redraws.
insights.quote: the way that any kind of animation works relates just three steps clearing the screen they're updating the sprites removing all those mobis around

insights.claim: Devine notes that Tetris was originally a terminal game, written in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov for a Soviet PDP-11 clone, the Electronika 60.
insights.detail: He wrote a terminal Tetris homage while commuting on Caltrain.
insights.quote: Tetris was written in as a terminal game so this was written in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov

insights.claim: To match NES Tetris frame timing in a terminal, Devine adds a fixed 60-frames-per-second timer to the clear-update-draw loop.
insights.detail: He timed all frames to be exactly those of NES Tetris. He says other approaches exist for sprites, but for blocky terminal movement a timer works best.
insights.quote: you also are going to introduce a timer

insights.claim: Unicode quadrant block characters give each terminal cell four independently lit 'pixels' (16 combinations), using foreground and background colours to draw higher-resolution sprites.
insights.detail: Devine's character sprite is 6 by 6 characters. Since he isn't an artist and has no drawing tool, he authors sprites as ASCII text and interpolates them into quadrant characters.
insights.quote: you can actually light up different quadrants of that character itself and there's 16 values

insights.claim: Quadrant-character graphics need a good monospaced font and adjusted line spacing, and work best on Linux; macOS and Windows terminals often break the line spacing.
insights.detail: Devine recommends iTerm2, which is GPU accelerated, and warns the code points require dealing with UTF-16 rather than UTF-8, which gets weird.
insights.quote: the key here is that you need a good font a good monospaced font you got to change the line spacing

insights.claim: Terminals' 256-colour palettes exceed 1980s 8-bit consoles, but each quadrant character can only show two colours and pixels are taller than wide, causing artifacting.
insights.detail: Devine's Text Invaders Space Invaders clone is playable in the terminal and can even be cut and pasted. The two-colour limit per cell and elongated pixels are the trade-offs of the technique.
insights.quote: you can only do in one of those four pixel characters you can only do two character or two colors

insights.claim: Devine's terminal recreation of Super Mario Bros level 1-1 stores the whole map in a text file and draws 16-by-16 sprites interpolated into quadrant characters.
insights.detail: Mario only walks through the level since Devine did not want to finish and be sued; it's not distributed for legal reasons, unlike his other Docker Hub demos.
insights.quote: I have the entire map of one one is is just like in a text file and it kind of works
